item.title: Breakfast Wrap: Furious escalation in One Nation’s “traitor” attack
item.description: Coverage and analysis of national and international events.

item.title: Breakfast Wrap: Government unveils digital duty of care laws
item.description:
The federal government has unveiled its proposed Digital Duty of Care, which it says builds on Australia's "world-leading" social media ban for children. The draft laws could let Australians opt in or out of algorithms used to push social media content.

Recap the morning's news, politics and global affairs with the Breakfast Wrap.

item.title: Breakfast Wrap: Can we switch off the algorithm?
item.description:
Can we simply shut off the algorithms sending content to our screens on the world's biggest social media platforms?

That is what the federal government would love to be able to do via new legislation its introducing this week. 

Then we'll dive into One Nation's new superannuation policy with MP Barnaby Joyce. 

And we'll hear about daring heists of food and beverage products in the United Kingdom.

Recap the morning's news, politics and global affairs with the Breakfast Wrap.

item.title: Breakfast Wrap: Germany's far right reaches new heights
item.description:
Exit polls show Germany's far-right AFD party has won its first state election in the country's east.

No far-right wing party has won a major election in Germany since World War Two.

But the party looks like it will fall just short of securing an absolute majority, so will it be able to form a coalition? 

Then - is there an anti boy ideology being taught in schools?

That's what the Nationals leader thinks, so we'll ask an expert who has contributed to the respectful relationships curriculum. 

The Ukrainian President has had a high level meeting with Trump's envoys in Kyiv, the day after they met with the Russian President. 

And the federal government responds to the Coalition's plans to cut the cigarette excise by 80%. 

Recap the morning's news, politics and global affairs with the Breakfast Wrap.

item.title: Breakfast Wrap: How unified is the Pacific?
item.description:
Fresh off the Pacific Islands Forum Leaders Summit, the Palau President is projecting unity, despite the summit being engulfed in tension.

There's been a number of notable absences, also the presence of Taiwans foreign minister, and a holdout over a statement criticising a recent Chinese missile test.

We'll hear from the President, and Australia's climate change mnister who was there too. 

Then the new ACTU Secretary talks housing. 

And we look back at the life and legacy of feminist icon  Gloria Steinem. 

Recap the morning's news, politics and global affairs with the Breakfast Wrap.

item.title: Breakfast Wrap: Unpacking Australia's economic growth
item.description:
It's not down, but it's barely up, and yet inflation remains a problem - so what is going on with the Australian economy right now?

The latest National Accounts data shows the economy growing by 2.1% over the year to June 30, but productivity remained sluggish. 

We hear from the Treasurer, the Shadow Treasurer and a panel of economists to unpack what it all means. 

Then we also head to Nepal to hear about the challenging work of recovering and identifying bodies being pulled from the disaster zone. 

Recap the morning's news, politics and global affairs with the Breakfast Wrap.

item.title: Breakfast Wrap: Nepal shifts to rehabilitation
item.description:
Four really insightful interviews spanning the disaster zone in Nepal, key court cases in the US, and a major political forum in the Pacific. 

Hear from a Nepali MP about the government's shift to rehabilitation. She tells us the government will still keep security forces in place to find any survivors. 

Then the whistleblower who contributed to the case against Meta thats seen the social media giant pay an $18bn settlement to US states. 

We'll also speak with the LAPD officer who investigated Tupac Shakur's murder. 

And the Pacific Affairs Minister Pat Conroy joins us from Palau amid a bumpy Pacific Islands Forum summit.

Recap the morning's news, politics and global affairs with the Breakfast Wrap.

item.title: Breakfast Wrap: The right to erasure
item.description:
The federal Attorney-General says you could soon exercise the 'right to erasure' and ask large digital platforms to destroy your personal information.

Under the government's proposal for new privacy protections, companies would no longer be able to justify collecting more information than they need.  

We'll hear from the Attorney-General and the Privacy Commissioner. 

Then a Melbourne based geologist and engineer is helping Nepali authorities try to save hundreds of workers trapped in hydro-project tunnels deep in the mountains following deadly floods last week. 

Recap the morning's news, politics and global affairs with the Breakfast Wrap.

item.title: Breakfast Wrap: One Nation wins in WA
item.description:
One Nation is celebrating another political win this morning, securing its first ever seat in the WA parliament via a by-election on the weekend. 

We hear from One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce about what it means for the party's fortunes elsewhere around the country. 

Then we get the latest on the flooding along the Nepal-Tibet border. 

And hear how a perfectly timed penguin conference could assist Australian scientists amid the onslought of bird flu in Australia. 

Recap the morning's news, politics and global affairs with the Breakfast Wrap.

item.title: Breakfast Wrap: Fears of further floods in Nepal
item.description:
As the death toll climbs, and more people remain unaccounted for following devastating flash floods along the Nepal-Tiben border, we hear scientists concerns that more flooding could be on the way.

One year ago geoscientist Dr Jakob Steiner prepared a report on glacial lake bursts for the Nepali government as part of efforts to prepare the country for future disasters. He says he's frustrated the government was not prepared for the flash floods.

On the Breakfast Wrap he explains the current thinking around what led to this disaster, and what could happen next. 

We also hear from the Foreign Minister Pennny Wong, the former Australian Ambassador to Nepal Felicity Volk, and feature a musical performance from Tibetan-Australian musician and composer Tenzin Choegyal.

Recap the morning's news, politics and global affairs with the Breakfast Wrap.

item.title: Breakfast Wrap: 'Himalayan tsunami' floods hits Nepal
item.description:
There are horrific scenes coming out of Nepal and southern Tibet - where powerful flash flooding has ripped through communities - destroying homes and roads and killing more than 160 people.

Nepali authorities say 34 Australians are among the more than 400 international tourists missing in this disaster.

Then we'll hear some fighting words from the former treasury boss Ken Henry about WA's attempts to keep its GST deal intact. He's call the deal stupid and criticised the Premier's response, after Roger Cook called the Productivity Commission 'east-coast clowns'.

Recap the morning's news, politics and global affairs with the Breakfast Wrap.

item.title: Breakfast Wrap: Remembering Dolly Parton, 'the queen of country'
item.description:
Over a career spanning decades, Dolly Parton amassed a legion of fans as a country music sweetheart and global superstar.

We look back on her career and musical legacy.

Then a Productivity Commissioner responds to the Western Australian Premier's comments calling the commission 'east-coast clowns' after its interim report recommended revising the 2018 WA GST deal.

Recap the morning's news, politics and global affairs with the Breakfast Wrap.

item.title: Breakfast Wrap: The plan to power data centres
item.description:
The federal government wants to settle new rules for how data centres use energy at national cabinet tomorrow. 

The government says it doesn't want a 'race to the bottom' where states are pitted against each other, competing for data centres. 

Then, we'll get the latest on Canada's trade war with the US and Washington's latest sanctions on Iran. 

The British Prime Minister heads to Kyiv bearing gifts. 

And questions are raised around lobbying rules in Australia's federal parliament. 

Recap the morning's news, politics and global affairs with the Breakfast Wrap.

item.title: Breakfast Wrap: How does One Nation's migration policy differ from Labor's?
item.description:
Today on the breakfast wrap - why South Australia's Chief Vet is 'not surprised at all' that a second long-nosed fur seal is suspected to have contracted H5 bird flu in South Australia.And - are One Nation's migration targets any different from Labor's?

Senator Pauline Hanson outlined her party's migration policy on social media, intervening after One Nation MP David Farley said his party's immigration target would not be "too different" to Labor's.

Plus, a trade war erupts between Canada and the united states - get the latest on what both leaders are saying and what it means for middle powers like Australia.Recap the morning's news, politics and global affairs with the Breakfast Wrap.

item.title: Breakfast Wrap: Israeli Ambassador defends investigation
item.description:
The Israel Defense Forces this week released its findings into its attacks which killed aid and medical workers in Gaza.

The Australian government yesterday expressed outrage that no criminal findings were made in the deaths of Australian aid worker Zomi Frankcom and her World Central Kitchen colleagues.

Yesterday, the Israeli Ambassador was called into a meeting with the Foreign Minister - amid calls for him to be expelled from the country.

Today on the Breakfast Wrap we hear his interview with Sally Sara in full.

Then, two other cases that won't be subjected to a criminal probe both involve workers from Médecins Sans Frontieres.

In November 2023, two people were killed when their MSF marked car was fired upon by members of the Israeli army.

Months later - in February 2024 - a tank fired on a house, killing two relatives of MSF staff, injuring six others.

The IDF found there were mitigating circumstances in both those cases - and won't take further action. 

The Australian MSF boss shares their perspective of the IDF's findings. 

Recap the morning's news, politics and global affairs with the Breakfast Wrap.

item.title: Breakfast Wrap: Australia 'outraged' after Israel closes investigation
item.description:
Foreign Minister Penny Wong has expressed outrage at Israel's decision to close an investigation on strikes that killed an Australian aid worker and her colleagues.

She says the timing is insulting to Zomi Frankcom's family and all Australians, after the government was informed shortly before a public announcement, and on World Humanitarian Day.

On The Breakfast Wrap we hear from independent UN Commissioner Chris Sidoti, and from the federal government.

Then, a powerful speech in parliament shines a spotlight on veteran's healthcare.

Recap the morning's news, politics and global affairs with the Breakfast Wrap.

item.title: Breakfast Wrap: Gambling reforms pass lower house
item.description:
Labor's gambling advertising bill has officially passed the lower house of parliament.

As well as the government and the Shadow Minister for Communications, we hear from two voices not too happy about the bill's passing. 

One, understandably, representing gambling companies. 

But the other, a Coalition  MP who crossed the floor to vote against the reforms, arguing they didn't go far enough. 

Then, how is the federal government trying to protect superannuation consumers?

And Andrew Hastie talks One Nation in WA. 

Recap the morning's news, politics and global affairs with the Breakfast Wrap.

item.title: Breakfast Wrap: What's the cost of early super access?
item.description:
One Nation wants to expand early access to superannuation for some Australians. 

Access is currently allowed in limited circumstances, with the Tax Office approving almost 68,000 applications for early access in 2024 to 2025.

Then, new restrictions on gambling advertisements are expected to pass parliament this week, with the government striking a tentative deal with the Coalition. 

Recap the morning's news, politics and global affairs with the Breakfast Wrap.

item.title: Breakfast Wrap: The great GST debate
item.description:
A new war of words has broken out between state and territory governments, after the Productivity Commission labelled the 2018 GST deal for Western Australia a "costly mistake".

The interim report from the Productivity Commission - released on Friday - found the deal has cost the federal budget $23-billion in its first 6 years, $22-billion of which had flowed to WA.

We hear from the former Finance Minister who was a key architect of the deal - Mathias Cormann. Then - the Treasurers of Western Australia, New South Wales and South Australia. 

As well as the GST carve up - we get into the announcement of a joint gun buyback scheme between NSW and the Federal Government.

Recap the morning's news, politics and global affairs with the Breakfast Wrap.

item.title: Breakfast Wrap: Five years from the fall of Kabul
item.description:
This weekend marks five years since Afghanistan's capital Kabul fell to Taliban forces.

We look back at the chaotic withdrawal of US troops, the end of a devastating war, and the repression that's followed. You'll hear from a former Afghan politician who fled to the US in 2021.

Then, why is Tasmania the last state to record a bird flu case.

And the count down is on to count Count Binface out of the race for Clacton - we'll get the latest on the by-election consuming British politics.

item.title: Breakfast Wrap: A radical plan for housing
item.description:
The shadow minister delivered a speech to the National Press Club yesterday in which he called for the National Construction Code to be cut from 2,000 to 80 pages. We hear from the shadow minister and the industry about his proposals. 

Then, what do you know about Australia's under-sea fibre optic cables? An expert explains why we need to do more to protect them.

Recap the morning's news, politics and global affairs with the Breakfast Wrap.

item.title: Breakfast Wrap: What is scandium?
item.description:
The US government has announced more than half-a-billion dollars in funding for a "world-first" mining project in central western New South Wales. We unpack why. 

Then, the Federal Treasurer discusses the RBA's latest decision on interest rates. 

We cover the latest in Colombia following this week's deadly earthquake. 

And a group is pushing for questions on allergies to be part of the next census.

Recap the morning's news, politics and global affairs with the Breakfast Wrap.

item.title: Breakfast Wrap: Colombia races to find quake survivors
item.description:
Colombia is racing to find survivors after a deadly earthquake hit the country. We'll take you there to hear about the community at the centre of the disaster.

Then, the South Australian State government has launched a new royal commission into artificial intelligence and the policy settings around it - the Premier Peter Malinauskas explains his thinking. 

And Federal Parliament resumes today, with the government hoping to pass a number of bills this sitting fortnight - including proposals to overhaul the National Disability Insurance Scheme and regulations around gambling.

Recap the morning's news, politics and global affairs with the Breakfast Wrap.

item.title: Breakfast Wrap: What Australia must do to tackle bird flu
item.description:
Are there things Australia can learn from the US in the fight against bird flu? 

Also, the government is determined to pass its reforms to the National Disability Insurance Scheme, but now a former director of the NDIA suggests a new approach is needed. 

And tomorrow night millions of Australians will fill in the census. With a selection of new questions on gender and sexuality, what will the latest figures be able to tell us? 

Recap the morning's news, politics and global affairs with the Breakfast Wrap.

item.title: Breakfast Wrap: ABC apologises to Gina Rinehart
item.description:
Did the ABC get it right on the Race Around the World controversy? 

We hear from the ABC's former editorial boss about an apology the broadcaster has made to Australia's richest person about a line in a short film aired on television. 

Then, we cap a big week of debate on gambling, with Independent Senator David Pocock and Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles. 

Recap the morning's news, politics and global affairs with the Breakfast Wrap.
